title: Reading a garment: seam allowances, necklines and sleeves

say: Reading a garment: seam allowances, necklines and sleeves.
This is the video for module 2 of Fashion Basics and Clothing Alterations.
Taking in is almost always possible. Letting out is limited by how much fabric is hidden inside the seams. Ten minutes of measuring saves you from promising a size the garment can never reach.

say: Seam allowance is the fabric between the stitching and the cut edge. Home patterns often use 1.5 cm. Ready-made clothes often use 1 cm or less.

panel.heading: Turn it inside out and look
items: Seam allowance: stitching to cut edge
Darts can be sewn narrower
Overlocked seams are usually trimmed narrow
A deep hem or wide centre back gives extra

say: A dart can be let out by sewing it narrower.

say: An overlocked seam is usually trimmed narrow, so there is little to let out.

say: A deep hem, a deep facing or a wide centre-back seam can give you extra fabric. Write down the allowance at every seam.

say: Every seam joins two layers. Move the stitching 1 cm outwards, and each panel gains 1 cm, so the circumference grows by 2 cm.

panel.heading: Can Bisi's skirt be let out?
items: Move a seam 1 cm: circumference grows 2 cm
Two side seams, 1 cm usable: 4 cm
Centre back, 0.5 cm usable: 1 cm
Total 5 cm: hip 106, not 107

say: You cannot use the whole allowance. Leave about 1 cm beyond the new stitching, and more on fabric that frays, or the seam will pull apart.

panel.rule: Leave at least about 1 cm of seam allowance after letting out.

say: For example, Bisi's skirt hip is 101 cm and she needs 107. Each side seam has 2 cm, so 1 cm is usable on each edge. Two side seams give 4 cm.

say: The centre back has 1.5 cm, so 0.5 cm is usable. That gives 1 cm more.

say: Total 5 cm. The hip can reach 106, not 107. You tell her honestly that it will be a little snug when sitting, or offer side panels from her leftover fabric. You do not promise 107.

say: When you let a seam out, the old stitching line becomes visible. On many cottons and ankara prints, the needle holes close after washing and pressing.
On satin, silk and coated fabrics they stay. So unpick 2 cm at the bottom of a seam, press it, and show her the mark in daylight. Let her decide before you go further.
A neckline can be lowered or reshaped, but raising one needs an added panel, because once you cut, the fabric is gone. Mark the new depth with her bra on, and check the straps are covered.

panel.heading: Lowering a round neckline
items: Mark the new depth on the client
Fold at centre front, cut both sides at once
Cut 1 cm outside the chalk line
Staystitch 1 cm from the new edge
New facing, clip the curve, understitch
Press and tack at the shoulders

say: Fold the garment at centre front and cut both layers together, so both sides match. Cut about 1 cm outside your chalk line for the seam.

say: Staystitch 1 cm from the new edge, from shoulder to centre front. This one line stops the curved edge stretching.

say: Cut a new facing, clip the curve every 1 to 1.5 cm, and understitch so the facing rolls inside. A garment with no opening must still go over her head, so measure first.

say: For example, Ifeoma's wide blouse sleeves catch on things when she cooks. One underarm seam has two layers, so you move the stitching half the reduction. At the upper arm, 7 cm less means moving 3.5 cm.

panel.heading: Narrowing wide sleeves
items: Upper arm: 44 minus 37 = 7 cm, move 3.5
Wrist: 30 minus 27 = 3 cm, move 1.5
Curve back to 0 at the underarm
Tack, try on, then sew

say: At the wrist, 3 cm less means moving 1.5 cm.

panel.heading: Narrowing wide sleeves
items: Upper arm: 44 minus 37 = 7 cm, move 3.5
Wrist: 30 minus 27 = 3 cm, move 1.5
Curve back to 0 at the underarm
Tack, try on, then sew

say: Curve the line back to the original seam below the underarm. If you carry it into the armhole, the sleeve pulls when she lifts her arm.

panel.heading: Narrowing wide sleeves
items: Upper arm: 44 minus 37 = 7 cm, move 3.5
Wrist: 30 minus 27 = 3 cm, move 1.5
Curve back to 0 at the underarm
Tack, try on, then sew

say: Check her hand passes through, tack the seam, and let her bend her elbow and lift her arms before you sew. Remember, a cuffed sleeve takes much longer to shorten, so price it accordingly.

say: Point the seam ripper away from your body and your other hand. Pushing it along a seam can slice the fabric. Keep rippers and scissors closed and away from children.

cards.d: Point it away from you. Cut every few centimetres, never push it along the seam.
Polyester can melt. Test on a seam allowance, use a pressing cloth.
Switch off and stand it upright when you walk away. Keep the cord out of the way.

say: Polyester and nylon can melt or go shiny under a hot iron. Test on a seam allowance and use a pressing cloth.

cards.d: Point it away from you. Cut every few centimetres, never push it along the seam.
Polyester can melt. Test on a seam allowance, use a pressing cloth.
Switch off and stand it upright when you walk away. Keep the cord out of the way.

say: Switch the iron off and stand it upright when you walk away, and keep the cord where nobody can trip or pull it down.

cards.d: Point it away from you. Cut every few centimetres, never push it along the seam.
Polyester can melt. Test on a seam allowance, use a pressing cloth.
Switch off and stand it upright when you walk away. Keep the cord out of the way.

say: To remember. Check the seams before you accept a letting-out job. Moving a seam 1 cm changes the circumference by 2. Keep about 1 cm safe. Staystitch and understitch a new neckline. And curve sleeve lines back before the armhole.
